tarr-coyne-wild-west-playground.html:
I was very disappointed that the Wild West Playground isn't actually Wild West themed. There are some round log stockades, and that's about it. I looked up pictures from before the 2015 renovation, and it used to look much more Western. That's a shame. At least there's almost no plastic. It's nearly all wood, and I like that.

It's one of many playgrounds along the west side of Central Park, near the West 93rd Street entrance, and one of several named after and funded by the Tarr family (see also Tarr-Coyne Tots and Tarr Family). Fun fact: the original 1988 design was by Richard Dattner, the same architect behind Adventure Playground.

The equipment is all a little… small. This playground is best for small kids, ages 2 to 5.

There are lots of chains, and I'm not sure what that's about. The tin-cans-on-a-chain thing is unique; I haven't seen one before. It's not all that fun, but at least it's novel.

The river down the middle is great. Kids love floating things down it. It's less a river and more a canal… which is exactly what they need at the Erie Canal Playground! Sure, it's turned off for half the year, but when it's dry it's fun to race trucks down. Fun for me, at least.
erie-canal-playground-dewitt-clinton-par:
First, the names. The park is DeWitt Clinton Park, on the far West Side of Hell’s Kitchen, and the playground inside it has its own name: The Erie Canal Playground. The Erie Canal was Mayor/Governor DeWitt Clinton’s magnum opus. The mules (not horses) are a canal reference, since mules towed the barges. But apart from three mules and a painted canal route on the ground, there’s really nothing canal-y about this playground. Don’t expect it to be like River Run – it only has a painted stream, instead of a real one.

The park even had a shot at naming the whole neighborhood: there was a push to rename Hell’s Kitchen “Clinton” after it, which never fully stuck, maybe because the park was so nasty back then. For decades it was notorious for being a late-night pickup spot for mixed-gendered people of the night, with drivers pulling in straight off the West Side Highway. It’s a very large park in a commercial part of town, so of course stuff went down here. These days it isn’t all that seedy anymore. People (with kids) are moving into the nice new condos overlooking the Hudson, and plenty of them use this as their neighborhood playground.

And now for the important part, the playground:

Surrounded by London plane trees on a rocky hill, with partial Hudson River and Midtown views, it’s actually kind of nice for a playground in a park with this kind of history.

It was built in 1996, and it’s held up… mediocrely. There are a couple of sinkholes with barricades around them. The original paint is gone or faded, with very poorly done layers of paint slathered on top. The sad mules got the same treatment, and they look sticky. Put your kid on them at your own risk; they may not unstick.
tarr-family-playground.html:
Tarr Family Playground sits on Central Park's West Side at 100th Street, and it's very easy to get to from Central Park West or the park loop. At first glance it looks like a pretty common playground. Look a little closer and there are some fun features: a spider web, a little jacks maze, and a bridge with lots of ways to climb over it. Some descriptions call the wooden structure a treehouse, but it's a far cry from a treehouse. It's fun, and it's partially made of wood, but that doesn't make it a treehouse.

I call this one the racetrack. A path wraps around the whole playground with a very fun swirl that takes kids down, around, and under a bridge, and kids on bikes love it. Keep an eye on toddlers, since the bikes are usually zooming around. If your kid is a little bigger, check that they can actually fit under the bridge. I've seen some head-bangers.

It's well laid out, with one entrance and exit and good visibility of the whole playground, except in the murder tunnel. The murder tunnel has blood stains. We just pretend it's a volcano and that's lava.

The playground first opened in 1973 as an adventure-style design, and the equipment is stamped 2008, right around when the Central Park Conservancy rebuilt it. It's very clean, it doesn't get too busy, and it usually has a nice crowd of upper UWS locals. The Tarr name is on three Central Park playgrounds (this one, Tarr-Coyne Tots, and Tarr-Coyne Wild West), so somebody in that family really likes playgrounds.

There are no bathrooms nearby that I know of. It's a bit of a hike to the nearest public restrooms in the park.
ancient-playground-central-park.html:
Ancient Playground has an awkward address. It sits in the traffic triangle where the 86th Street Transverse meets Fifth Avenue, right beside the Met. You can see traffic on every side and hear the horns while you play. You also can't get in from the park; you need to walk in from Fifth Avenue after playing some pretty hairy Frogger.

The name oversells it. “Ancient” makes you picture pyramids and temples. What you get is a lot of concrete and brick in a drab, brutalist style, plus two concrete obelisks that are apparently meant to go with that other obelisk in the park, the one Egypt didn't exactly hand over. The theming just feels a little phoned in. The toddler area is a sandpit with an awkward concrete slide thing under one of the obelisks. I do like that there's basically no plastic, apart from two tire swings.

But here's the thing: this is the best playground in the city for playing tag. I've been pulled into games with the bigger kids more than once, and I can bound onto and over the pyramids, but I get destroyed in the tunnels. The park is full of little structures that kids climb or run up, then slide or jump down the other side, and some of them have secret tunnels. Heckscher and Adventure Playground have similar structures, but these are exactly the right size for tag: regular, freeze, or the-ground-is-lava.

It's also great for climbers. My daughter named the saggy climbing rope the “bonky rope,” because kids flop around on it and bonk their heads. Overall this playground has held up fairly well, which is the upside of building with concrete, brick, and stainless steel. The trapeze rings have gone missing, and the rubber floor has a lot of patches.

It's usually clean, and it has its own private bathroom with separate Boys and Girls entrances inside the playground. IRL it's not nearly as haunted-looking as in this picture.
swedish-cottage-marionette-theatre.html:
This one isn't a playground, but it's a kid activity worth knowing about. The Marionette Theatre lives inside a very cool old building, the Swedish Cottage: a model schoolhouse built for the 1876 World's Fair in Philadelphia that has been put to all sorts of uses in Central Park over the years. It just got a new cedar shingle roof, which smelled great. Unfortunately, the outside was covered in scaffolding, so you'll have to take my word on how charming it is.

We saw Little Red's Hood, an updated Little Red Riding Hood. Red's a city kid addicted to her phone, Grandma's a spunky visitor to NYC, and the wolf is some kind of escaped lab animal who loves cupcakes. Familiar, but with a twist – like a cupcake. Or Toy Story 5.

It's a real, live marionette show, which is pretty cool. You can see the strings, and the theater is small and old-fashioned in the best way. The show runs about half an hour, and at the end the puppeteers do a little demonstration of how the marionettes work. The one strange part is that all the lines and songs are pre-recorded, so there's a disconnect between the live movements and the canned soundtrack. This is my biggest gripe about the whole thing. It just didn't really feel like live theater without real human voices.

Most kids in the audience were between 3 and 7. There's mixed information out there on whether little kids are free, but I can confirm infants don't need a ticket. My 3½-year-old enjoyed it a lot. Out of about 30 kids, 3 cried and had to be taken outside, which seems like a pretty normal rate for a dark room and a wolf.

Apart from the pre-recorded audio, here's my one real complaint: it started almost 15 minutes late. I showed up 15 minutes early expecting a prompt start, so we sat around twiddling thumbs for a very long time. At least we got the best seats.
domino-park-playground.html:
Domino Park stretches along the Williamsburg waterfront where the Domino Sugar Refinery once stood, and it has a series of playgrounds right on the water with amazing views of the Manhattan skyline. The equipment is a little different from what you'll see elsewhere; it blends right into the industrial look of the old refinery. The main playground, by artist Mark Reigelman, follows the sugar-making process: kids go in as raw sugar cane and come out the other end as sugar cubes. My daughter did not know that, and did not need to.

The clubhouse structures are tall and enclosed, so visibility for parents is low. There's only one entrance, though, so there's nothing to worry about. Except, possibly, the spider-web net inside a mock industrial vacuum, where a kid can get stuck. Pro tip: there's a way to fish a kid out through the bottom. I know because I had to do it.

Don't miss the mist bath along the water, where a cloud of fog seems to rise up from waves crashing on the rocks below. On a hot day it's magic. The splash pad has jets that fire at random, and kids love tearing through them trying to guess which one goes next, while parents enjoy a big seating area right alongside.

The bathrooms are a bit of a walk across the street, but they're large individual stalls and they're spotless. There's plenty for parents to do nearby, and some days there's even a farmers market.

Verdict: very high marks. Worth the trip from anywhere in the city.
adventure-playground-central-park.html:
Adventure Playground sits on a secluded hill near Central Park's West 67th Street entrance, just up the path from Tarr-Coyne Tots and a short walk from Tavern on the Green. Because it's tucked away, crowds and tourists don't wander in; it's mostly local Lincoln Square and southern Upper West Side families. Think of it as a smaller, quieter Heckscher: similar equipment, smaller scale.

It has a great backstory. The plaque says it was built in 1966, designed by architect Richard Dattner as one of New York's very first “adventure playgrounds.” It only exists because of a fight: in 1956, a group of Upper West Side moms stood their ground against Robert Moses, who wanted to cut down trees here for a Tavern on the Green parking lot. The moms won, and this corner of the park got an adventure playground instead. Good job, moms.

I love that there's no modern plastic equipment at all. It's stainless steel, concrete, granite, and sand, which is probably why it has held up so well for sixty years. Sure, technically there is a modern & safe rubber ground mat throughout the playground, but I'll let that… slide. Some noteworthy play pieces: a long fire pole (yes, fun for dads too, as demonstrated by my dad-bud), hidey castles, a very steep short and wide slide, and a little river running from the splash pad to the little series of drains.

It's a very nice secluded spot on a hill with mature trees all around, including an epic ash tree. There aren't many ash trees left of this size. The shade is lovely, but for some reason this place is mosquito central in summer. Bring bug spray.

On weekends, expect to see a birthday party or two. The inside scoop is that the city doesn't hand out fines for setting up small tables here the way it does at some higher-visibility spots.
heckscher-playground.html:
Heckscher is the OG, but not necessarily the GOAT. Known simply as “The Heck,” it's Central Park's oldest playground, opened in 1926, and at 1.8 acres, its largest. For my circle of parents, it's the default place for families to meet up. Everyone knows where it is, and everyone can find a spot.

The highlight is the castle-like stone structures with a little stream running through them. Following the stream from the drain all the way up to its source on Umpire Rock is fun for everyone, grown-ups included. You can even follow the stone causeway right up onto Umpire Rock itself, but I wouldn't recommend it for kids: there's usually broken glass up there from people drinking.

For some reason, my daughter's favorite part of this entire playground is a sewer drain just outside the sandbox. You can see water down below, and she'll stare into the abyss for ten minutes at a time. I wonder what she sees down there. Or what sees her.

Now for why we usually avoid it. Its central location in a very touristy area means it gets visited by all kinds of riff-raff. Even though it's huge, it's normally pretty darn busy. They call it “The Heck.” After the Saturday crowds, I have a few other names for it, but this is a family site. For some reason, it also attracts the kind of crowd that plays music out loud from their phones and leaves Dorito bags behind. During the week, it's full of nannies letting kids romp around. Keep an eye out, too: there are a few entrances and exits that kids can sneak out of. The bathrooms are attached to the playground, but they're shared with everyone in the park, so they can be pretty scuzzy.

Our most recent visit was a rainy Saturday in September, and the whole place was completely deserted, which was both fun and eerie. Verdict: still very much worth visiting for its sheer size and the view of the skyscrapers along Billionaires' Row. Just go on an off day if you can.
billy-johnson-playground.html:
Here's one many Manhattan parents have walked right past. Billy Johnson Playground is tucked into Central Park near East 67th Street, and you can't see it from Fifth Avenue or from the jogging loop. I've mentioned it to plenty of fellow parents who had no idea it existed. If Heckscher is too busy or just not your style, this is the place to go — it's sort of the East Side's answer to the Adventure Playground on the West Side.

It was designed back in the 1980s to feel like a miniature version of the park around it, and it shows. There's no truly original equipment here, but there's a picturesque little stone bridge (a kid-sized cousin of Gapstow Bridge down at the Pond), a long granite slide set right into a rocky hill, and a nicer-than-average splash pad. Regulars bring a piece of cardboard to sit on for extra speed on the slide. Take the tip.

The best trick is under the bridge. Water jets are built into the pathway there, which makes a fun little stretch to run through over and over again. And there's always a certain kind of kid — I was one of them — who waits for some unsuspecting soul to stroll under the bridge, then hits the button and cackles as the jets go off. It never stops being funny.

The tire swing is where kids learn to share and make friends. There's also a nice flat, open sandy area that's perfect for a game of kickball. Line of sight isn't great with all the rocks and plantings, but there's only one entrance and exit, so there's nothing to worry about.

Verdict: a genuine hidden gem. I'm not sure I'd cross the city just for it, but if you're anywhere on the East Side, it's a lovely way to spend an afternoon.
pier-6-brooklyn-bridge-park.html:
Pier 6 is one of NYC's latest and greatest, and it isn't really one playground. It's a group of medium-sized playgrounds all next to each other — Slide Mountain, Swing Valley, Sandbox Village, and the Water Lab — that add up to an amusement park. Having separate zones feels more fun than one giant play area. It feels like an adventure going from one to the next and finding more fun stuff around every corner.

In the slide park, there are some steel slides that give Slide Hill a run for its money. The curl at the bottom of the pyramid slide looks totally rad. Unfortunately, the slide just doesn't generate enough speed to send kids around the berm, so they slowly slide to a stop and fall off the side. Still fun, just not as fun as it looks.

The impromptu trails through the bamboo in the slide park were super popular among kids, mine included. Nobody designed them; kids just made them, which is the best kind of playground feature. Swing Valley was more serene than fun, and the one exception to the crowds.

The splash pad, rebranded the “Water Lab,” was the busiest zone, and for good reason: it's unlike any other splash pad in the city. It's built into the side of a rocky hill, with lots of original water features, including an Archimedes screw that kids can crank to lift water uphill.

It was very busy when we visited on a weekend, with barely any room for parents to sit on the sidelines. This park is so far out there, I was surprised to find so many people. It's an interesting mix: some foreign tourists, some day-trippers from other parts of the city like us, and some locals. The bathrooms are on the pier nearest the Water Lab, which can be a bit of a hike from the slides on the other side.
pier-97-playground.html:
Pier 97 opened recently, right on the Hudson near 59th Street. The star is the big slide, which you can only reach by climbing a tall ropes course in the middle of the playground. I've seen more than a few kids get scared and stuck up there, needing a parent to talk them (or carry them) down. I actually like that. Too many modern playgrounds feel way too safe and boring, and a little fear is good for the soul.

Farther back on the pier, past the playground, there's a ball field and some spots to hang out. There's also a wide granite slide for “all ages” that's short but fast. It gets very hot in the sun, so expect lots of burned butt cheeks in July. There's a grassy slope where the grown-ups can relax and tan.

Unfortunately, this place badly needs better upkeep. So many pieces of this brand-new equipment are already broken, and I've yet to see anything fixed. I've been turned away by the staff during posted hours and kicked out “for maintenance,” yet I'm at a loss to see what's being maintained. There's always garbage in the sand. Last time we went, a water gun, the water pump, and a sand scooper were all broken. The bike repair station just outside was a terrific idea, but its tools were broken or missing within weeks and never replaced. And the bathrooms, though very close by, are somehow always closed. Pier 97 staff, please get your act together!

One bonus: there's free kayaking very nearby, and it's well worth coordinating with a visit.

Verdict: go for the big slide. Climb up, slide down a few times, and move on.
imagination-playground.html:
I'd read all about this one before we went. Designed by the architect David Rockwell, Imagination Playground opened in 2010 with a big idea: instead of fixed equipment, give kids loose parts — giant foam blocks, crates, wagons — and let them build their own play. We showed up on a beautiful Sunday ready to build.

There were no blocks. No foam, no crates, no loose parts of any kind, nothing like the descriptions I'd read. The interesting-looking tubes and pipes scattered around turned out not to do anything at all. The only thing to play with was our imagination. So technically, the name is accurate.

The design isn't without charm. The whole playground is loosely boat-shaped and nautical, which suits the setting nicely, with the Seaport's old ships and the ferries right next door. There's a splash pad, though a pretty minimal one. And there's a bathroom right inside the playground, which deserves real credit, even if it was only moderately scuzzy.

The place was deserted the entire time we were there. As we were leaving, another family arrived — they'd taken the ferry over from Brooklyn specially — and they were every bit as disappointed as we were to find it empty and seemingly abandoned. I felt for them.

Verdict: best avoided, at least until someone brings the blocks back. If you're downtown, the Battery Playscape is a short walk away and a much better use of a Sunday.
the-yard-governors-island.html:
We found this one by accident, biking around Governors Island one weekend and wondering why a long line of families was queued outside a fence. On the other side was The Yard, run by a nonprofit called play:groundNYC, and it is certainly unique.

The best description I can offer: imagine some college kids went out on trash night, grabbed every old toy, plastic playset, tire, board, and pipe that looked fun, and dumped it all in a vacant city lot. Then imagine they handed that lot to children. That's roughly the idea, and it's a great one. It's a junkyard, and honestly? One man's trash is my kid's treasure. And then my laundry problem. It's an “adventure” or “junk” playground, where trained playworkers keep watch and kids climb, dig, and poke around in whatever happens to be lying there.

Logistics matter here. Everyone signs a waiver to get in. Parents wait outside the fence while chaperones keep an eye on things inside — which feels strange for about five minutes and wonderfully freeing after that. There's a little-kids zone and a big-kids area. We didn't qualify for the big-kids side, but I peeked through, and it looked way more fun. Admission is free; they ask for donations, and it's worth putting something in the jar.

Now the honest part: it is really scuzzy. Weeds, muddy puddles, and actual garbage are part of the experience. But isn't that exactly what was fun when you were a kid? My daughter, as it turns out, was kind of grossed out, and I still can't decide whether to be proud or disappointed.

Verdict: definitely worth the trip, unless you're afraid of grime, splinters, booboos, or things of that nature. Pack clothes you don't love and a sense of adventure.
slide-hill-governors-island.html:
Slide Hill is exactly what it sounds like: a bunch of metal slides built into the side of a hill on Governors Island. And it's great, because it does this one thing very, very well. There's a short fat slide, a long thin slide, and a few in between, including one wide enough for two to ride down together. Four slides and a hill. Which way down? That's a slippery question.

I personally prefer the granite slides at the Battery Playscape, but these are longer. In fact, the longest slide in all of New York City is right here, 57 feet from top to bottom. (For the fastest slide in the city, see Chelsea Waterside.)

Half the fun is getting to the top, because there are multiple ways up. You can climb the stone steps, follow a well-landscaped winding path, or clamber up the wooden beams terracing the slope. Every kid we saw had a favorite route, and most of them changed it every lap.

If you've never been to Governors Island with kids, it's worth a trip, and this is a great stop while you're there. It's an easy ride on the ferry, which seems to be free on weekend mornings. Time your visit with a stop at The Yard: most of the families we saw on Slide Hill headed straight over as soon as The Yard opened.

Verdict: worth the trip, especially as part of a full day on the island.
river-run-playground.html:
This playground is aging, but it's great. It's a true hidden gem: you can't see it from any road, so you have to wander through Riverside Park to find it. That's a treat in itself, because the landscaping around here is first-rate, and there's a very cool giant boulder along the way.

What makes River Run unique is its centerpiece: a replica of the Hudson River running right through the middle. “Replica” is being generous — it's really a squiggly concrete stream — but it's a lot of fun. It starts at a splash-pad fountain and winds its way down to a drain near the sandbox. Who doesn't want to float an impromptu boat all the way down it? We floated a leaf all the way down the river. It was a moving experience. Mostly for the leaf.

The other highlight is the legendary sandbox, with its so-bad-they're-great faces molded into the sides by a local artist. I know a few parents who are genuinely creeped out by them and avoid the sandbox completely. I think they're great. There's also a large public restroom right within the park, which is worth its weight in gold.

I disapprove of the modern plastic equipment that's crept in here: a few plastic pieces and one weird blue modern climber that don't really jive with the rest of the place. But I'm impressed there's a seesaw, since there are so few left in playgrounds anywhere. I suppose the newer pieces add variety, since a stream isn't everyone's idea of fun (and it gets turned off in the winter). Good news for the future: after a community outcry, the city's planned renovation will keep both the river and the sandbox sculptures.

Verdict: worth traveling to. Because it's a bit older, it often gets overlooked, which is exactly why it deserves a visit.
classic-playground-riverside-park.html:
I got genuinely excited about this one. Seesaws are an endangered species in New York City playgrounds, and here was a whole collection of them, plus an honest-to-goodness metal jungle gym, the kind that taught my generation about gravity. It sits right on the Hudson River Greenway near 74th Street, which ought to mean river views and a nice breeze.

Unfortunately, this playground seems to have been abandoned by the Parks Department. The view of the water is blocked by maintenance equipment. Weeds grow everywhere. Paint is flaking off in large chunks. About half the seesaws are missing entirely.

The big splash pad in the middle wasn't working, looked nasty, and had a garbage can parked across the entrance, which is about as clear a message as a playground can send.

One bright spot: the sycamore trees overhead shed their bark all over the ground, and stomping on it turned out to be a genuinely fun game of its own. Kids will find the fun anywhere, bless them.

Verdict: great concept, awful playground. The city should either give this place a little TLC to make it amazing again, or close it and move that classic equipment to parks where it'll get used and cared for. Until then, best avoided.
safari-playground-central-park.html:
Some playgrounds you plan a whole Saturday around. Safari Playground is not one of those, and that's perfectly fine. It's the one we coast into halfway through a jogging-stroller lap of Central Park, right about when somebody in the stroller announces that it is her turn to run. Perched on a little hill near West 91st Street with the Reservoir just past the fence, it's a very pleasant place to be told that.

The theme is a river full of hippos. Big hippos surface out of a blue rubber “river,” some yawning, some just eyes and ears poking up, and a couple of play canoes are beached along the banks. Kids take to the whole setup instantly: the hippos are for climbing, and the canoes are for paddling to wherever a four-year-old needs to go that day. The Conservancy rebuilt the place in 2019 and cast new hippos from molds of the old ones, but they've been loved hard since. Several are showing their age, with duct tape patching holes in the fiberglass. Nobody under three feet tall seems to mind.

Here's the insider tip. At the north end there's a rubbery mound with one really steep side. Officially it's landscaping. Unofficially it's the best feature in the place: kids will spend ages sprinting up it, sliding back down, and trying again. It is, and I say this with real affection for the slide nearby, more fun than the actual slide.

The splash pad is about average — push the button, get sprayed, repeat. And there are no bathrooms, which is the thing to plan around. Bring a child who has already gone, or know your route to the nearest park facilities before you commit.

Verdict: not worth crossing the city for, but if you're passing by, stop. It's a fine neighborhood stop, but not a hidden gem and not a destination.
pier-51-playground.html:
Pier 51 is like a smaller and more modern version of River Run, built out on a pier. It's newer, cleaner, and more colorful. Like River Run, it has a stream running through the middle — this one is a nod to Minetta Brook, an old Manhattan stream that still runs underground — with little bronze fish, turtles, and crabs set along the way.

Kids love that stream. They dam it up with sand, float things down it, and then dam it up again. It's hydraulic engineering for the preschool set, and it can keep a crew busy for a long time.

It sits just a little south of Little Island, and it's actually hard to find on the map because it gets confused with its famous neighbor. Once you're on the right pier, you'll see it.

Being on a windy pier and built around water features, I can't imagine it would be much fun at all when it's cold out. This is a summer playground through and through.

Verdict: if you're in the area, it's worth stopping. But it's kind of small, so I wouldn't go out of my way to check it out.
battery-playscape.html:
The Battery Playscape opened at the southern tip of Manhattan in late 2021, and it was worth every year of the wait. It's big — a full acre and a half — and it's laid out as a string of landscapes rather than a jungle gym in a rubber square: bluffs, a riverbed, a marsh, dunes, and a meadow, all designed to flood and bounce back, since the Battery has seen its share of storm surges.

The slides may be the best in the city. They're polished granite, set into a rocky bluff, and they are fast. Big kids treat the tall ones like a racetrack, little ones get a baby slide of their own, and more than a few parents looked tempted. I went down the slide “to test it for safety.” Then I tested it eleven more times.

There are treehouses, rope bridges, climbing towers, sand and water play, and odd little discoveries tucked around corners. For us, the surprise hit was the little stage — a small theater built right into the playground. My daughter put on a show for an audience of one tired dad, and I'd buy a ticket again.

Afterward, the SeaGlass Carousel is right nearby, and it's gorgeous: you ride inside glowing fish. That's a perfect end to the outing.

The one catch: the bathrooms were closed for renovations, and the nearest open ones were a bit of a hike. Plan ahead. Verdict: highly recommended.
chelsea-waterside-playground.html:
I'll just say it up front: this is one of my favorite playgrounds of all time, and a real hidden gem. It's mostly locals, plus the occasional line of daycare kids from Chelsea Piers, and it rarely feels overrun.

The centerpiece is a giant, colorful wooden pipefish (a real Hudson River species) coiled around a tower. Inside that tower is one of the tallest slides in the city, and definitely the fastest. I've watched plenty of confident kids reach the top, look down, and quietly take the stairs back. The fish comes from the same Danish company that built the sturgeon at the Science Playground on Pier 26. This pipefish pre-dates the sturgeon, and its age shows a little bit. Perhaps this was the test, and it worked so well they decided to SCALE it up with the massive sturgeon.

The splash pad is a bit different from the usual, with big stone bull heads that spout water and little snail jets for the toddlers. Those bulls are real limestone carvings salvaged from an old Hell's Kitchen slaughterhouse, which is exactly the kind of history that makes a playground stick with you.

My only beef is the name. Chelsea Waterside isn't actually on the water. It's near the water: you have to cross 12th Avenue and walk a bit more to reach the river. Maybe that's why it stays a secret — the name sends people looking in the wrong place.

The bathroom is just outside the playground gate, which every parent will appreciate. Verdict: high ratings across the board. It's a hidden gem if you live nearby, and worth the trip if you don't.
margaret-kempner-playground.html:
I'd seen this one out of the corner of my eye a hundred times while running the Central Park loop, so I finally had to check it out. First challenge: getting in. The entrance is very hard to find from the Fifth Avenue side, and we did a lap of the fence before we spotted it.

Once inside, there are some fun log obstacles to climb over, balance on, and generally conquer, plus a strange rope obstacle that I still can't fully explain. Kids figured it out immediately, as kids do. If yours is a climber, it's worth a stop.

Attached to the playground is a secluded, wooded picnic area. It's a lovely idea. Unfortunately, it seems to double as a bathroom, because there are no actual bathrooms nearby. Your nose will tell you which corners to avoid.

The parents are mostly Upper East Side locals who tend to keep to themselves, which makes for a calm, if not especially chatty, afternoon.

Verdict: just okay. A fine stop for climbers when you're already in the neighborhood, but not one to plan a day around.
dinosaur-playground-riverside-park.html:
With a name like Dinosaur Playground, expectations run high in our house. We arrived at Riverside Park and 97th Street ready for a prehistoric adventure.

The reality: about half the playground is fenced off because of a sinkhole — one that, from what I've read, dates back to Hurricane Ida in 2021. The part that's open is in rough shape. With half of it fenced off, this place is well on its way to extinction.

The namesake dinosaurs, a fiberglass triceratops and a hadrosaur, are the only unique feature, and they have holes in them. Honestly, they look like they were built by a high school art class. They're not impressive in any way, which is a strange thing to say about a playground named after them.

Like the Classic Playground downriver, this one feels as though the city gave up on it. The good news is that a big renovation has been designed and approved, with more dinosaurs and better drainage. The less-good news is that it hasn't happened yet.

Verdict: very low ratings for now. We'll happily come back when the new dinos arrive.
balsley-park.html:
Every review site needs a floor, and Balsley Park is ours. The park itself is a small plaza on Ninth Avenue. Tucked inside is a gated kids' area, and inside that gate you'll find the entire play offering: two lumpy orange things.

That's it. Two. I've seen more excitement in a bowl of oatmeal. You can sit on them. You can stand on them, briefly. My daughter gave them an honest try, because she's a good sport, and then looked at me as if to ask what we were really doing here.

The kids' area is gated off from the rest of the park, which should make it a safe little haven. In practice, every time we've come by, it's been occupied by people sleeping rough or teenagers smoking weed. I have never once seen another kid in there.

I don't enjoy writing reviews like this. This neighborhood needs good places for kids to play, and this spot could be one with some real equipment and a little attention. But as it stands, it earns the lowest rating possible across the board.

Verdict: best avoided. If you're nearby, walk to the Tom Otterness Playground on 42nd Street or head into Central Park instead.
tom-otterness-playground.html:
If you've ever waited for the A train at 14th Street and noticed little bronze figures getting up to mischief around the station, you already know Tom Otterness. Now picture one of his guys supersized to about 30 feet long and stretched out in a garden at the foot of the Silver Towers on West 42nd Street. His legs are slides. His arms are for climbing. His head is a lookout. It's public art you are allowed — encouraged, even — to go down headfirst.

My daughter named it “The Big Guy and Little Guys Playground” on our first visit, because small bronze figures are hidden all over the sculpture, and finding them became a quest. I don't think we've found them all. I'm not sure anyone has.

The playground itself isn't big. The metal dude is just about all there is, plus a little kids' playground right next to him. But it's a lot of fun precisely because nothing else in the city is quite like it. The two leg-slides are made for racing, and it's very hard not to declare a best-of-seven.

It's clean, and it's usually pretty quiet — the far-west end of 42nd Street isn't on anyone's way to anywhere, which is exactly why it stays a gem. The only real downside is bathrooms: there aren't any. I believe the nearest public facilities are across 12th Avenue along the river in Hudson River Park.

Verdict: a true hidden gem. Pair it with a stroll up the river greenway and you've got a lovely morning.
pier-26-science-playground.html:
This is a great multi-zone playground, and it's definitely worth the trip. The highlight is the pair of giant sturgeon — an Atlantic sturgeon and a shortnose sturgeon, both endangered Hudson River natives — built by the same Danish company that made the pipefish at Chelsea Waterside. They're fun for kids and for active parents alike. Playgrounds are more fun when they don't feel too much like playgrounds. No kid (or adult for that matter) wants to be told how to have fun. Playing on these massive fish feels like you're doing something slightly wrong. In any other setting you'd get scolded for climbing all over a sculpture. But here, it's all OK. Awesome. You can even clamber right onto the top and ride one like a seahorse.

Kids crawl through the sturgeon's insides, and spill out like caviar. Which leads to a local tradition: the lost-child panic. There's always a dad shouting “Hudson!” or “Ava!” or “Jaxerton!” into a fish while his kid plays happily somewhere in the tail. For the record, parents do fit inside. But know going in that line of sight is limited, so this isn't the place to sit on a bench and scroll Instagram.

Around the sturgeon are more fun things: climbing nets, rubbery lumps, and misters that make a cloud of steam around some sculpted shrimp. The regular playground next door is pretty darn fun too. It has most of the usual stuff, including a splash pad, plus a delightfully off-kilter merry-go-round of sorts. There are serviceberry trees planted around, and in spring they have edible berries. Be prepared for weird looks, but they're delicious.

Right in the middle, between the fish and the other playground section, there's a public bathroom, which every parent will appreciate. On top of all that, there's a mini golf course, an oyster bar on a boat, and volleyball courts nearby, so the grown-ups are well looked after.

Verdict: worth the trip. The only downsides are that it's a little hard to get to, and it gets extremely busy on weekends. Go early.
tarr-coyne-tots-playground.html:
This is a little playground just for toddlers, right next to the Adventure Playground in Central Park. We came here a lot when my daughter was learning to walk, and honestly, this playground helped her take her first steps. That alone earns it a soft spot in my heart.

The whole ground is covered in soft rubber, with little lumps sticking up for toddlers to grab, pull themselves up on, and then try to toddle over to the next one. It's like a training course for walking. All the tots seem to instinctively make their way up the rubber mountain and perch at the top. Thankfully, they don't know how to play king of the hill yet.

There are also swings, a sandbox, and a water sprayer (I wouldn't call it a full splash pad). Since there's a bigger and more exciting playground right next door, there aren't any rowdy big kids running around here. Just toddlers. And lots of pacifiers.

Expect local Upper West Side parents calmly hanging out with babies from about six months to two years old. When nature calls, the bathrooms are in Tavern on the Green, a few hundred feet away.

Verdict: it suits its purpose perfectly, but don't expect anything too exciting. Once your little one is walking with confidence, graduate to the Adventure Playground next door.
